title: India pitches a 50 billion euro trade goal with Italy, about 3.5 times last year's trade
subtitle: Piyush Goyal raised the idea in Rome on 18 November. Here is how India and Italy trade today and how the India and EU deal fits in.
content_html:
Picture a cricket side chasing 20 runs, and the captain suddenly says: why not go for 50? On Wednesday, 18 November 2026, India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal did something like this with Italy. In Rome, he called for raising the India and Italy trade target to 50 billion euros. Last year, goods trade between the two countries was 14.25 billion euros. So the new idea is about three and a half times last year's level.

The euro is the money used in Italy and most of Europe. Here is what the talks were about, what India and Italy sell to each other, and why this matters for small Indian makers.

First, what is a trade target?

Trade between two countries is simple to count. Add up everything India sells to Italy and everything Italy sells to India in one year. That total is the trade between them.

A trade target is a goal for that total, like the run target in a cricket chase. It tells officials, banks and business groups which way to push. India and Italy already have one. After the two countries raised their ties to a "Special Strategic Partnership" in May 2026, they started working towards 20 billion euros a year by 2029. The commerce ministry says this goal is part of a Joint Strategic Action Plan for 2025 to 2029.

Going from 14.25 billion euros to 20 billion euros means a rise of about 40%. Mr Goyal now wants both sides to think much bigger. In his words, they "should not limit the numbers". He gave no year for the 50 billion euro goal. He spoke of it for "the years to come".

Where did this happen?

Mr Goyal was in Italy on 17 and 18 November. He held talks with Antonio Tajani, Italy's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister. The two co-chaired the 23rd meeting of the India and Italy Joint Commission for Economic Cooperation. Think of this commission as a regular review meeting, where both sides check how trade and investment are doing and fix the next steps. The last one was held in Brescia, Italy, in June 2025.

The same day, Rome hosted the India and Italy Business and Innovation Forum. Its sessions covered car parts, food processing machines, medicines and chemicals, and clean energy, plus a special session for startups. There, young firms could meet investors and research centres from Italy.

This video from Italy's foreign ministry shows the joint press conference after the talks.

The goods the two countries sell to each other

Italy is India's fourth largest trading partner in the European Union. From April to August 2026, sales from India to Italy grew by 29.9% to $3.92 billion compared with the same months a year earlier. Note that this number is in US dollars, while the targets are in euros.

According to the commerce ministry, the main goods going from India to Italy are:

  • iron and steel, and metal products
  • electrical and electronic equipment
  • chemicals
  • textiles and clothes

Coming the other way, India mostly buys machinery and electrical equipment, chemicals and metal products from Italy. So India sends a lot of materials and clothes, and Italy sends a lot of machines. Each side buys what the other is good at making.

How the India and EU trade deal fits in

An FTA, or free trade agreement, is a deal where countries cut the import duty they charge on each other's goods. An import duty is a tax paid when goods enter a country. Say an Italian shop buys shirts from India and pays a duty of 10 euros on a 100 euro order. If the duty falls to zero, the same order costs the shop 100 euros instead of 110. Indian shirts become cheaper on Italian shelves, and the shop may order more.

India and the European Union, the group of European countries that includes Italy, finished talks on their FTA in January 2026. Mr Goyal said the deal is likely to be signed in December and could take effect in the first three months of next year. He said it would make trade easier for businesses in both countries.

Before the visit, Mr Tajani wrote that the deal will lower tariffs in areas like industrial and farm machinery, packaging, car parts, chemicals and medicines. A tariff is another word for an import duty.

Why should a small Indian maker care?

Two kinds of trade matter most here. India buys machinery from Italy, and Indian mills and workshops sell textiles, clothes and metal goods there.

Mr Goyal gave real examples. The Italian firm Danieli has projects worth 500 million euros from SAIL, the state steel maker. These will bring Italian green steel technology to more than 4 million tonnes of steelmaking capacity in India. He also pointed to the fashion brand Prada working with Indian artisans to make Kolhapuri sandals. And he called Tata Motors taking control of the Italian truck maker Iveco last month the largest ever Indian investment in Italy.

Mr Tajani wrote that around 1,000 Italian companies already operate in India, many with factories here. He also said Italy will soon open an Italian Innovation Centre in India for startup programmes and joint research.

What else did India ask for?

Trade is not only about duties. Rules and paperwork matter too. According to The Economic Times, India:

  • asked Italy to help Indian shipyards get approval from the European Commission to break and recycle old ships for European needs
  • wants to be recognised as a place where waste and scrap from Europe can be sent for recycling
  • is looking at faster certification and approvals for Italian firms in India, and wants similar help for Indian firms in EU countries, where approvals for some products can take a long time

Mr Tajani said Italy sees scope in space, defence, steel and manufacturing, and that two planned task forces would help remove barriers that firms face.

What happens next?

The 50 billion euro figure is only an idea for now, not a signed goal. The goal both governments have written down is still 20 billion euros by 2029. Before the visit, Mr Goyal noted that trade between the two countries had doubled in 10 years.

The big thing to watch is the India and EU trade deal. If it is signed in December and starts early next year, Italian buyers may find Indian goods cheaper. Factories in India may also find Italian machines cheaper. For a young person thinking of a small export business, in clothes, metal goods or chemicals, Italy is one market worth reading about.
